paragraphs: When Swamiji spoke about the women of India, he liked to point to warriors as well as saints.

He reminded his listeners of Lakshmi Bai, the Queen of Jhansi. During the uprising of 1857 she fought the English soldiers and held her ground for two years. She led modern armies, handled the artillery herself, and always charged at the very front of her troops. And this fearless commander, Swamiji noted, was a Brahmin girl.

Swamiji knew an old soldier who had lost three of his sons in that war. When he spoke of his sons he stayed calm. But when he spoke of the Rani, his voice came alive. He called her a goddess, not a human being, and said he had never seen better generalship in his life.

Swamiji then recalled Chand Bibi, also called Chand Sultana, who lived from 1546 to 1599 and is remembered as the Queen of Golconda, the land of the diamond mines. When her city was besieged, she defended it for months. Finally the enemy broke a hole in the walls and the imperial army tried to pour through. Chand Bibi met them there in full armour and forced them back.
The book adds that the soldiers were so impressed by her courage and military skill that they gave her the title Chand Sultana, meaning Chand the Empress.
learn: Courage and leadership have never belonged to one gender. These women led from the front when it mattered most. Whoever you are, do not let anyone's narrow idea of what people like you can do decide how far you go.
